data.reason: Under the K1 reading the main goal is on_time_deliveries, with p95_wait_s, max_wait_s and unfinished as customer monitors. Option 1 raises mean on-time from 223.6 to 225.2 (+1.6), but only 2/5 seeds improved, so on most seeds it did not help the main goal. That is not enough evidence to override a majority 'no' vote by B and C. Its customer monitor gains are real but small: p95_wait_s 116 → 108, max_wait_s 154 → 141, and unfinished stays 0.0 either way. Its costs are measured and larger: road violations rise from 18.2 to 24.0 (about +30%), B's utility falls from 69.8 to 61.4, and C's falls from 58.2 to 46.0. C has already lost from D1. Fairness between companies is not part of the KPI as read in K1, so it is not the deciding reason. It is the tie-breaker when the KPI gain itself is not robust. The current rules already deliver 223.6 on time with only 4.4 late and 0.0 unfinished. Keeping v2 follows the LLM's recommendation and the vote outcome. I reject option 2 (hold_limit 60s → 50s), which was not offered for adoption: it lowers on-time by 1.0 (0/5 seeds) and worsens max_wait_s. block_k 3 → 2 should be measured again under the next period's demand before it is reconsidered.
assumptions: The 5-seed measurement is representative of period 2 conditions (normal + rush demand).
The rise in road violations from 18.2 to 24.0 carries some real cost to other road users or safety, even though the table does not say what kind.
A 13 s drop in max wait and an 8 s drop in p95 wait is a modest customer benefit, not a decisive one, given 0.0 unfinished and few late deliveries now.
unknowns: Whether the +1.6 on-time gain of block_k 2 holds over more seeds or under heavier demand.
Why B and C lose utility under block_k 2.
Next period's demand level and congestion.
Whether the extra road violations matter for safety.
